subject: computer-science

moments.title: Babbage describes the Analytical Engine
moments.body: Babbage publishes the first detailed description of his Analytical Engine — a mechanical, general-purpose, programmable computer using punched cards adapted from the Jacquard loom. It would have had a 'store' (memory), 'mill' (CPU), conditional branching, and looping.
moments.takeaway: A general-purpose programmable computer was theoretically described 109 years before the first one ran.

moments.title: Lovelace's notes on the Engine
moments.body: Lovelace translates Luigi Menabrea's French paper on the Analytical Engine and adds 'Notes' three times its length. Note G describes an algorithm to compute Bernoulli numbers — often cited as the first published algorithm intended for a machine. Lovelace also speculates the Engine could compose music or manipulate symbols beyond numbers.

quote.text: The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform.
quote.attrib: Ada Lovelace, Notes on the Analytical Engine, 1843

moments.takeaway: Lovelace grasped that programmability meant the machine was about manipulating symbols, not just calculation.

now.title: Mechanical computing today
now.body: Babbage's Difference Engine No. 2 was finally built by the Science Museum, London, in 1991 (calculating part) and 2002 (printer) — and worked. The Analytical Engine was never built. Ada (the language, 1980) is named for Lovelace; the 'Ada Lovelace Day' second Tuesday of October celebrates women in STEM.
now.open_questions: Why did it take until the 1940s to realise mechanically what Babbage described? Funding, manufacturing tolerances and the absence of a clear market all played roles.

reflection: Computing has always had visionaries who saw the destination before the technology existed to take them there. Lovelace's reach beyond pure calculation prefigures the symbolic-AI debates of a century later.
